---
title: "Checking occJSDM against simulated truth"
description: >
  How accurately occJSDM recovers parameters it is given, and how honest the
  credible intervals around them are. Measured on 1000 simulated datasets
  across ten scenarios, plus a per-species occupancy check.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# Every number in this article is rendered from dev/simstudy/validation-data.rds,
# written by dev/simstudy/export_validation_data.R from a run of
# dev/simstudy/run_study.R. Nothing here is typed in by hand.
#
# It used to be. The article was 882 lines of hand-transcribed HTML, which cost
# hours to update, could not be checked against the data it described, and went
# stale invisibly when six commits landed under it between the run and the
# reader. If you find yourself about to type a number into the prose below,
# that is the regression this setup exists to prevent -- put it in the bundle
# and reference it.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, results = "asis", message = FALSE,
                      warning = FALSE)

# pkgdown knits articles with the working directory set to the article's own
# directory, plain rmarkdown from wherever the caller happens to be. Resolve
# against both rather than assuming either.
vd_path <- local({
  # Walk up looking for DESCRIPTION rather than taking an rprojroot dependency
  # for six lines; articles must build with nothing beyond what the package
  # already needs.
  root <- normalizePath(".", mustWork = FALSE)
  for (i in 1:6) {
    if (file.exists(file.path(root, "DESCRIPTION"))) break
    parent <- dirname(root)
    if (identical(parent, root)) break
    root <- parent
  }
  cands <- c(file.path(root, "dev/simstudy/validation-data.rds"),
             "dev/simstudy/validation-data.rds",
             "../../dev/simstudy/validation-data.rds")
  hit <- Filter(file.exists, cands)
  if (length(hit) == 0L)
    stop("validation-data.rds not found. Run dev/simstudy/run_study.R, then ",
         "Rscript dev/simstudy/export_validation_data.R.")
  hit[1]
})
vd <- readRDS(vd_path)

# --- formatting helpers --------------------------------------------------

`%||%` <- function(a, b) if (is.null(a)) b else a

fmt <- function(x, d = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
pct <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

#' Write raw HTML into the document, stripping leading indentation first.
#'
#' Not cosmetic. A `results='asis'` chunk hands its output to pandoc as
#' markdown, and markdown reads any line indented four or more spaces as a
#' code block -- so indented HTML comes out the far side escaped, as visible
#' `&lt;p&gt;` in the page rather than a paragraph. Templates below are indented
#' to match the surrounding markup for readability, so they must be de-indented
#' on the way out.
emit <- function(x) cat(gsub("(?m)^[ \t]+", "", x, perl = TRUE))

#' Emit one HTML table in the report's own styling.
#'
#' `flag` marks a whole row; `lo` marks individual cells. Both take predicates
#' over the data frame so the thresholds live with the data rather than being
#' baked into the markup, which is how the shaded rows in the old hand-written
#' table drifted out of step with the numbers beside them.
html_table <- function(df, caption = NULL, digits = NULL,
                       flag = NULL, lo = NULL, align_first_left = FALSE) {
  cols <- names(df)
  digits <- if (is.null(digits)) setNames(rep(3L, length(cols)), cols) else digits

  cell <- function(v, col, i) {
    classes <- "num"
    if (!is.null(lo) && isTRUE(lo(df, col, i))) classes <- paste(classes, "lo")
    txt <- if (is.numeric(v)) fmt(v, digits[[col]] %||% 3L) else as.character(v)
    if (align_first_left && col == cols[1]) sprintf("<td>%s</td>", txt)
    else sprintf('<td class="%s">%s</td>', classes, txt)
  }

  body <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(df)), function(i) {
    tds <- paste0(vapply(cols, function(cn) cell(df[[cn]][i], cn, i), ""),
                  collapse = "")
    cls <- if (!is.null(flag) && isTRUE(flag(df, i))) ' class="flag"' else ""
    sprintf("<tr%s>%s</tr>", cls, tds)
  }, "")

  paste0(
    '<div class="scroller"><table>',
    if (!is.null(caption)) sprintf("<caption>%s</caption>", caption) else "",
    "<thead><tr>",
    paste0(vapply(seq_along(cols), function(j)
      if (align_first_left && j == 1L) sprintf('<th class="lbl">%s</th>', cols[j])
      else sprintf("<th>%s</th>", cols[j]), ""), collapse = ""),
    "</tr></thead><tbody>",
    paste0(body, collapse = ""),
    "</tbody></table></div>")
}

# --- figures --------------------------------------------------------------
#
# These were four committed PNGs until 10 August 2026, drawn once and then left
# behind by every subsequent run -- the same staleness problem as the tables,
# just harder to notice because a plot does not look wrong when it is out of
# date. They are drawn from the same bundle as everything else now.

library(ggplot2)

# Deliberately neutral: the surrounding report supplies its own palette and the
# figures should not fight it. Reads in both pkgdown themes because it commits
# to neither, using mid-tone greys that hold against a light or dark ground.
theme_val <- theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9.5),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 9.5),
        plot.margin = margin(4, 8, 4, 4))

#' Coverage with a binomial interval, which the old static figures drew but
#' never documented. n_checked is the number of interval decisions behind each
#' point, so the error bar shrinks where a block has more elements.
cov_se <- function(p, n) sqrt(pmax(p * (1 - p), 0) / pmax(n, 1))

# Order blocks consistently everywhere, so the eye can move between figures.
block_order <- function(x) {
  ref <- vd$summary[vd$summary$scenario == vd$example_cell, ]
  lev <- ref$block[order(ref$coverage)]
  factor(x, levels = union(lev, sort(unique(x))))
}

#' One panel per parameter block, one point per scenario.
plot_by_block <- function(what) {
  d <- vd$summary
  d$value <- d[[what]]
  d$block <- block_order(d$block)
  ggplot(d, aes(x = value, y = scenario)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
               colour = "grey45", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_point(size = 1.7, colour = "grey20") +
    facet_wrap(~ block, scales = "free_x") +
    labs(x = what, y = NULL) +
    theme_val
}

#' Coverage per block, pooled across scenarios, against the nominal 0.95.
plot_coverage_by_block <- function() {
  d <- vd$summary
  d$block <- block_order(d$block)
  d$se <- cov_se(d$coverage, d$n_checked)
  ggplot(d, aes(x = coverage, y = scenario)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed",
               colour = "grey45", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = coverage - 1.96 * se,
                       xmax = coverage + 1.96 * se),
                   height = 0, colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_point(size = 1.7, colour = "grey20") +
    facet_wrap(~ block) +
    labs(x = "coverage (dashed line = nominal 0.95)", y = NULL) +
    theme_val
}

#' Distribution of psi_cor across every species-fit, for two survey sizes.
#'
#' Drawn as a distribution rather than as means because the means understate
#' what changes. The top of the range barely moves -- species already recovered
#' well were near the ceiling -- and almost the whole gain is in the left tail,
#' i.e. in how often a species comes out unusable. A mean hides that entirely.
plot_sites_distribution <- function() {
  ex <- vd$extra_cells[["sites_300"]]
  if (is.null(ex)) return(NULL)
  b <- vd$occupancy[vd$occupancy$scenario == vd$example_cell &
                    !is.na(vd$occupancy$share_lat), ]
  s <- ex$occupancy[!is.na(ex$occupancy$share_lat), ]
  if (nrow(b) == 0 || nrow(s) == 0) return(NULL)

  d <- rbind(
    data.frame(arm = "100 sites", psi_cor = b$psi_cor, share_lat = b$share_lat),
    data.frame(arm = "300 sites", psi_cor = s$psi_cor, share_lat = s$share_lat))
  d$arm <- factor(d$arm, levels = c("100 sites", "300 sites"))

  # Bands cut on the pooled distribution so both arms are split identically.
  br <- stats::quantile(d$share_lat, 0:4 / 4)
  band_lab <- c(
    sprintf("Occupancy mostly explained by MEASURED covariates (unmeasured share under %.0f%%)", 100 * br[2]),
    sprintf("Mostly measured (unmeasured share %.0f to %.0f%%)", 100 * br[2], 100 * br[3]),
    sprintf("Mixed (unmeasured share %.0f to %.0f%%)", 100 * br[3], 100 * br[4]),
    sprintf("Occupancy mostly explained by UNMEASURED factors (share over %.0f%%)", 100 * br[4]))
  d$band <- cut(d$share_lat, br, include.lowest = TRUE, labels = band_lab)

  top <- sprintf("EVERY species-fit: %s datasets x %d species, each survey size",
                 format(length(unique(b$replicate)), big.mark = ","),
                 length(unique(b$species)))
  pd <- rbind(transform(d, panel = top),
              transform(d, panel = as.character(band)))
  pd$panel <- factor(pd$panel, levels = c(top, band_lab))

  mu <- aggregate(psi_cor ~ arm + panel, pd, mean)
  mu$lab <- sprintf("mean %.2f", mu$psi_cor)

  ggplot(pd, aes(psi_cor, fill = arm, colour = arm)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey35", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.32, linewidth = 0.55, adjust = 1.1) +
    geom_vline(data = mu, aes(xintercept = psi_cor, colour = arm),
               linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.45, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(data = mu, aes(x = psi_cor, y = Inf, label = lab, colour = arm),
              vjust = 1.35, hjust = -0.1, size = 2.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
    facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("100 sites" = "#8C8C8C",
                                 "300 sites" = "#1F5F6B"), name = NULL) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("100 sites" = "#5A5A5A",
                                   "300 sites" = "#1F5F6B"), name = NULL) +
    labs(x = paste("How well the species was placed across sites:",
                   "1 = perfectly, 0 = no information about where it is,",
                   "below 0 = worse than guessing"),
         y = "share of species-fits",
         caption = paste("Solid line at 0 marks the no-information point.",
                         "Dashed lines are arm means.")) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.6, 1)) +
    theme_val +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 8.6, hjust = 0),
          legend.position = "top",
          axis.title.x = element_text(size = 8.6),
          plot.caption = element_text(size = 7.3, colour = "grey45", hjust = 0))
}

#' The transpose: one panel per scenario, one point per block.
plot_coverage_by_scenario <- function() {
  d <- vd$summary
  d$block <- block_order(d$block)
  d$se <- cov_se(d$coverage, d$n_checked)
  ggplot(d, aes(x = coverage, y = block)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed",
               colour = "grey45", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = coverage - 1.96 * se,
                       xmax = coverage + 1.96 * se),
                   height = 0, colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_point(size = 1.7, colour = "grey20") +
    facet_wrap(~ scenario) +
    labs(x = "coverage (dashed line = nominal 0.95)", y = NULL) +
    theme_val
}
```

```{=html}
<div class="occjsdm-report">
<style>
.occjsdm-report {
  --ground:      #F5F6F4;
  --ground-sunk: #ECEEEA;
  --rule:        #D3D8D2;
  --ink:         #15202B;
  --ink-soft:    #4E5B62;
  --ink-faint:   #7C878C;
  --accent:      #1F5F6B;
  --good:        #3E7D5A;
  --warn:        #A06A1B;
  --bad:         #9E3A2E;
  --good-fill:   #C5D8C9;
  --bad-fill:    #E3C0B8;

  --serif: "Iowan Old Style", "Palatino Linotype", Palatino, Georgia, serif;
  --sans:  system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;
  --mono:  ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, "SF Mono", Menlo, Consolas, monospace;

  background: var(--ground);
  color: var(--ink);
  font-family: var(--sans);
  font-size: 17px;
  line-height: 1.65;
  -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;
  border-radius: 8px;
}

/* Synced to pkgdown's own light/dark toggle (data-bs-theme on <html>)
   rather than the OS preference, so this block always matches the rest
   of the page regardless of which one the reader has set. */
html[data-bs-theme="dark"] .occjsdm-report {
  --ground:      #12181C;
  --ground-sunk: #1A2126;
  --rule:        #2C3740;
  --ink:         #E4E9E7;
  --ink-soft:    #A6B2B6;
  --ink-faint:   #77848A;
  --accent:      #6BB3BF;
  --good:        #74B48C;
  --warn:        #D3A245;
  --bad:         #DC8371;
  --good-fill:   #2E4638;
  --bad-fill:    #4E2E29;
}

.occjsdm-report .wrap {
  /* Widened twice. 45rem -> 58rem because the 5-7 column tables were hitting
     the .scroller fallback constantly; 58rem -> 74rem because the figures
     are the widest thing here now and were being squeezed, and because at
     58rem the page reads narrow against the whitespace around it.
     Paragraphs keep their own cap below, so line length stays readable and
     only the tables and figures take the extra room. */
  max-width: 74rem;
  margin: 0 auto;
  padding: 3rem 1.5rem 4rem;
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  gap: 3.25rem;
}

.occjsdm-report .eyebrow {
  font-family: var(--mono);
  font-size: 0.7rem;
  letter-spacing: 0.14em;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  color: var(--accent);
}

.occjsdm-report h1 {
  font-family: var(--serif);
  font-size: clamp(2.1rem, 5.5vw, 3rem);
  line-height: 1.1;
  font-weight: 600;
  letter-spacing: -0.015em;
  text-wrap: balance;
  margin: 0.5rem 0 0;
}

.occjsdm-report .standfirst {
  font-family: var(--serif);
  font-size: 1.2rem;
  line-height: 1.55;
  color: var(--ink-soft);
  margin: 1rem 0 0;
  max-width: 34rem;
}

.occjsdm-report h2 {
  font-family: var(--serif);
  font-size: 1.6rem;
  font-weight: 600;
  line-height: 1.2;
  letter-spacing: -0.01em;
  text-wrap: balance;
  margin: 0;
  padding-top: 1.5rem;
  border-top: 1px solid var(--rule);
}

.occjsdm-report h3 {
  /* Was 0.95rem sans, i.e. SMALLER than the 17px body text and in a
     different family from h1/h2 -- so subheadings read as bold paragraphs
     rather than headings, and "Does a bigger survey help?" disappeared into
     the prose around it. Now serif like the other headings and clearly
     above body size, sitting between h2's 1.6rem and the text. */
  font-family: var(--serif);
  font-size: 1.4rem;
  font-weight: 600;
  line-height: 1.25;
  margin: 0.6rem 0 0;
  letter-spacing: -0.005em;
}

.occjsdm-report section { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 1.1rem; }
/* Prose keeps its own cap well inside .wrap: a 74rem-wide paragraph is
   unreadable however wide the page is. 46rem is roughly 80 characters at
   this size, which is the top of the comfortable range. */
.occjsdm-report p { margin: 0; max-width: 46rem; }

/* knitr wraps every chunk figure in a <p>, so the prose cap above was
   squeezing the generated plots to 46rem inside a 74rem column -- which is
   why they rendered small and hard against the left margin rather than
   filling the space. Figures are not prose and take the full column. */
.occjsdm-report p:has(img) { max-width: none; text-align: center; }
.occjsdm-report img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; display: block;
                      margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto; }
.occjsdm-report strong { font-weight: 650; }
.occjsdm-report code {
  font-family: var(--mono);
  font-size: 0.86em;
  background: var(--ground-sunk);
  padding: 0.1em 0.34em;
  border-radius: 2px;
}

/* ---- the tally: coverage made visible ---- */
.occjsdm-report .tally-set { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 2rem; }
.occjsdm-report .tally { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 0.75rem; }

.occjsdm-report .tally-head {
  display: flex;
  align-items: baseline;
  justify-content: space-between;
  gap: 1rem;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
}

.occjsdm-report .tally-label { font-size: 0.92rem; color: var(--ink-soft); }
.occjsdm-report .tally-label b { color: var(--ink); font-weight: 650; }

.occjsdm-report .tally-delta {
  font-family: var(--mono);
  font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums;
  font-size: 0.78rem;
  color: var(--ink-faint);
  letter-spacing: 0.02em;
}

.occjsdm-report .tally-row {
  display: grid;
  /* First column is sized for a short caption. Do not put long parameter names
     here: beta_theta needs 73px against this column's 58, and widening it
     pushed the whole row past 375px on a phone. Parameter names go in the
     .tally-label, which wraps. */
  grid-template-columns: 3.6rem 1fr 3.2rem;
  gap: 0 0.9rem;
  align-items: center;
}

.occjsdm-report .tally-when {
  font-family: var(--mono);
  font-size: 0.66rem;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  letter-spacing: 0.09em;
  color: var(--ink-faint);
}

.occjsdm-report .tally-score {
  font-family: var(--mono);
  font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums;
  font-size: 0.95rem;
  font-weight: 600;
  text-align: right;
}
.occjsdm-report .tally-score.is-good { color: var(--good); }
.occjsdm-report .tally-score.is-warn { color: var(--warn); }
.occjsdm-report .tally-score.is-bad  { color: var(--bad); }

.occjsdm-report .marks {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(25, 1fr);
  gap: 3px;
}
@media (max-width: 34rem) { .occjsdm-report .marks { grid-template-columns: repeat(20, 1fr); } }

.occjsdm-report .marks.is-before { opacity: 0.42; }
.occjsdm-report .mark { aspect-ratio: 1; border-radius: 1px; }
.occjsdm-report .mark.hit  { background: var(--good-fill); }
.occjsdm-report .mark.miss { background: var(--bad); }

.occjsdm-report .tally-note { font-size: 0.85rem; color: var(--ink-faint); margin: 0; }

/* ---- tiers ---- */
.occjsdm-report .tiers { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 0; }

.occjsdm-report .tier {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 4.5rem 1fr;
  gap: 0 1.25rem;
  padding: 1.15rem 0;
  border-bottom: 1px solid var(--rule);
  align-items: start;
}
.occjsdm-report .tier:first-child { border-top: 1px solid var(--rule); }

.occjsdm-report .tier-when {
  font-family: var(--mono);
  font-size: 0.72rem;
  line-height: 1.5;
  color: var(--accent);
  letter-spacing: 0.03em;
  padding-top: 0.15rem;
}
.occjsdm-report .tier-body { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 0.35rem; }
.occjsdm-report .tier-body p { font-size: 0.92rem; color: var(--ink-soft); }

/* ---- tables ---- */
.occjsdm-report .scroller { overflow-x: auto; }
.occjsdm-report table { border-collapse: collapse; width: 100%; font-size: 1rem; }
.occjsdm-report caption {
  text-align: left;
  font-size: 0.95rem;
  color: var(--ink-faint);
  padding-bottom: 0.6rem;
}
.occjsdm-report th, .occjsdm-report td {
  /* Centred, not left. Numbers left-aligned under a left-aligned header
     read as ragged text rather than as a column of values. Label cells opt
     back out below. */
  text-align: center;
  padding: 0.55rem 0.9rem;
  border-bottom: 1px solid var(--rule);
  vertical-align: top;
}
.occjsdm-report th {
  font-size: 0.82rem;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  letter-spacing: 0.08em;
  color: var(--ink-faint);
  font-weight: 600;
  border-bottom-color: var(--ink-faint);
}
/* The label column: html_table() emits it as a bare <td> and marks its
   header th.lbl. Both stay left-aligned; everything else centres. */
.occjsdm-report th.lbl, .occjsdm-report td:not([class]) { text-align: left; }

.occjsdm-report td.name { font-family: var(--mono); font-size: 0.82rem; white-space: nowrap; }
.occjsdm-report td.num  { font-family: var(--mono); font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }

.occjsdm-report tr.flag td { background: var(--ground-sunk); }
.occjsdm-report td.num.lo { color: var(--bad);  font-weight: 650; }
.occjsdm-report td.num.hi { color: var(--accent); font-weight: 650; }

/* ---- callouts ---- */
.occjsdm-report .pending {
  border-left: 3px solid var(--accent);
  padding: 0.9rem 0 0.9rem 1.1rem;
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  gap: 0.5rem;
}
.occjsdm-report .pending p { font-size: 0.92rem; color: var(--ink-soft); }

.occjsdm-report .finding {
  border-left: 3px solid var(--warn);
  padding: 0.9rem 0 0.9rem 1.1rem;

}
.occjsdm-report .finding p { font-size: 0.92rem; color: var(--ink-soft); }
.occjsdm-report .finding h3 { color: var(--ink); }

.occjsdm-report .fig {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  gap: 0.6rem;
}
.occjsdm-report .fig img {
  width: 100%;
  height: auto;
  border-radius: 6px;
  border: 1px solid var(--rule);
  /* the PNGs are rendered on a fixed white background; a light card behind
     them keeps that from looking like a mistake against a dark page */
  background: #fff;
  padding: 0.5rem;
}
.occjsdm-report .fig figcaption {
  font-size: 0.95rem;

}

.occjsdm-report footer {
  border-top: 1px solid var(--rule);
  padding-top: 1.25rem;
  font-size: 0.82rem;
  color: var(--ink-faint);
}
</style>
```

```{=html}
    <h1>Checking occJSDM against simulated truth</h1>
    <p class="standfirst">
      Two questions, asked of the same model: how close its estimates are to the truth,
      and how honest the uncertainty around them is. Neither answer implies the other,
      and this package is currently better at one than the other.
    </p>
  </header>

  <section>
    <h2>The trick behind every test</h2>
    <p>
      All of it rests on one idea: <strong>make fake data where we already know the
      right answer.</strong> <code>simulateOccJSDMData()</code> lets us choose the true
      species coefficients, the true detection rates, the true everything &mdash; then
      generate a dataset from them.
    </p>
    <p>
      We hand that dataset to <code>runOccJSDM()</code>, which knows none of it, and
      check whether it finds its way back. Real data can never do this. You never know
      the true occupancy of a species at a site, so you can never tell whether the model
      got it right.
    </p>
    <p>
      Everything below is one of two questions. <strong>Is the estimate close?</strong>
      That is accuracy, and it comes first. <strong>Is the stated uncertainty
      honest?</strong> That is calibration, and it comes second. A model can pass either
      while failing the other, and this one does exactly that in places.
    </p>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>Recovering occupancy, species by species</h2>
    <p>
      Start with the thing an occupancy model exists to do: say where each species is.
      One fit of a hundred sites and ten species, two chains of 500 iterations after 500
      discarded. Source: <code>tests/testthat/test-recovery-occupancy.R</code>.
    </p>
```

```{r species-example}
ex <- vd$species_example
cat(html_table(
  ex[, c("species", "occ_true", "occ_est", "psi_cor", "auc",
         "drv_cov", "drv_err")],
  caption = sprintf(paste("One row per species from a single fit: replicate %d",
                          "of the <code>%s</code> cell. Shaded rows fall below",
                          "a threshold used by one of the checks below."),
                    vd$example_replicate, vd$example_cell),
  digits = list(species = 0, occ_true = 2, occ_est = 3, psi_cor = 3,
                auc = 3, drv_cov = 3, drv_err = 3),
  flag = function(d, i) d$psi_cor[i] < 0.30 || d$auc[i] < 0.60,
  lo = function(d, col, i) {
    (col == "psi_cor" && d$psi_cor[i] < 0.30) ||
    (col == "auc" && d$auc[i] < 0.60)
  }))
```

```{=html}
    <p>
      <b>occ_true</b> is the fraction of the hundred sites where the species really is
      present; <b>occ_est</b> is the fraction where the model thinks it is. Close values
      are necessary but not sufficient: a model can get the overall prevalence right
      while placing the species at entirely the wrong sites.
    </p>
    <p>
      <b>psi_cor</b> catches that. It correlates the estimated chance of presence against
      the true chance across sites, so it asks whether the species is put in the
      <em>right places</em> rather than merely the right number of them. It runs from
      &minus;1 to 1, and 0 means the estimates say nothing about where the species is.
      <b>auc</b> asks the same question more forgivingly: the chance the model rates a
      site where the species really is present above one where it really is absent. A
      coin flip scores 0.5.
    </p>
    <p>
      The last two columns concern the coefficients underneath. Each species has three
      -- a baseline and two environmental effects. <b>drv_cov</b> is the share whose
      stated range contains the true value, and <b>drv_err</b> is the average distance
      from best guess to truth, on the coefficients&rsquo; own scale, so there is no fixed
      good value.
    </p>
```

```{r worst-species}
# The narrative used to name species 6 and quote its numbers by hand, which
# meant it silently described the wrong row the moment the study was re-run.
# Find the weakest row instead, and say only what the data supports about it.
w <- ex[which.min(ex$psi_cor), ]
rank_err <- rank(-ex$drv_err)[which.min(ex$psi_cor)]
ord <- c("worst", "second worst", "third worst")[rank_err]

emit(sprintf('
    <p>
      <strong>Species %d is the row to read twice.</strong> Its <code>psi_cor</code>
      of %s and <code>auc</code> of %s say the model has barely located it%s.
      %s
      That pairing between a poor estimate and honest uncertainty about it is the
      reason this article asks two questions rather than one, and it recurs at grid
      scale further down.
    </p>',
  w$species, fmt(w$psi_cor), fmt(w$auc),
  if (!is.na(ord)) sprintf(", and its <code>drv_err</code> is the %s here", ord)
    else "",
  if (w$drv_cov >= 0.99)
    sprintf(paste("Yet <code>drv_cov</code> is a perfect %s, because the intervals",
                  "on its coefficients are wide enough to contain the truth anyway."),
            fmt(w$drv_cov))
  else
    sprintf(paste("Its <code>drv_cov</code> of %s says the intervals on its",
                  "coefficients do not fully absorb that either."),
            fmt(w$drv_cov))))
```

```{=html}
    </p>
```

```{r across-replicates}
# This section is new, and it exists because the sentence it replaces was an
# admission: "a single fit cannot say whether that is a property of the model
# or the luck of one dataset." The study fits every cell 100 times and now
# scores occupancy on all of them, so the question is answerable rather than
# rhetorical. One table of ten species becomes a distribution over hundreds.
os <- vd$occupancy_summary
cell <- os[os$scenario == vd$example_cell, ]
prev <- vd$occupancy_by_prevalence
prev_cell <- prev[prev$scenario == vd$example_cell, ]

emit(sprintf('
    <h3>Is that species unlucky, or is the model?</h3>
    <p>
      The table above is one fit. It cannot tell you whether a weak row is a
      property of the model or the luck of one dataset -- so the study fits the
      same cell %d times and scores every one. That turns ten numbers into
      <b>%s species-fits</b>, and the question becomes answerable.
    </p>
    <p>
      Across those, <code>psi_cor</code> averages <b>%s</b>, with the middle 90%%
      running from %s to %s. The single fit above is therefore %s. %s
    </p>',
  cell$R, format(cell$n_species_fit, big.mark = ","),
  fmt(cell$psi_cor_mean), fmt(cell$psi_cor_q05), fmt(cell$psi_cor_q95),
  if (abs(mean(ex$psi_cor) - cell$psi_cor_mean) < 0.05) "typical"
    else if (mean(ex$psi_cor) > cell$psi_cor_mean) "a little better than typical"
    else "a little worse than typical",
  sprintf(paste("A weak row like species %d sits inside that spread rather than",
                "outside it, so it is the ordinary variation between species and",
                "datasets, not a defect."), w$species)))

if (!is.null(prev_cell) && nrow(prev_cell) > 1) {
  cat(html_table(
    prev_cell[, c("prevalence", "n_species_fit", "occ_true",
                  "psi_cor_mean", "psi_cor_q05", "psi_cor_q95", "auc_mean")],
    caption = sprintf(paste("Occupancy recovery banded by how common the species",
                            "actually is, over all %d replicates of",
                            "<code>%s</code>. The q05 and q95 columns are the",
                            "middle 90%% of species-fits in each band."),
                      cell$R, vd$example_cell),
    digits = list(prevalence = 0, n_species_fit = 0, occ_true = 3,
                  psi_cor_mean = 3, psi_cor_q05 = 3, psi_cor_q95 = 3,
                  auc_mean = 3),
    align_first_left = TRUE))

  best <- prev_cell[which.max(prev_cell$psi_cor_mean), ]
  worst <- prev_cell[which.min(prev_cell$psi_cor_mean), ]
  # Is the relationship monotonic in prevalence, or humped? This decides which
  # claim the paragraph can honestly make. The first full run showed a hump:
  # recovery climbs from the rarest band, peaks in the middle, then eases off
  # for the commonest species -- which is why the plain correlation between
  # prevalence and recovery is near zero while the bands plainly differ.
  # Quoting that correlation as "rare species are harder" would contradict the
  # table directly above it.
  humped <- which.max(prev_cell$psi_cor_mean) < nrow(prev_cell)

  n_rarest <- prev_cell$n_species_fit[1]
  emit(sprintf('
    <p>
      <strong>Prevalence looks like it matters. It mostly does not.</strong>
      Species in the %s band average %s, the weakest here, against %s in the
      strongest band (%s), which invites the reading that rare species are the
      hard ones. Two things argue against it. The weakest band rests on %d of
      the %s species-fits in this cell, so it is the noisiest number in the
      table. And across all of them the plain correlation between how common a
      species is and how well it is placed is <b>%s</b> -- essentially nothing.
    </p>
    <p>
      An earlier version of this page read the bands as evidence that the model
      struggles with rare species. That does not survive a proper look: the
      next section finds what actually drives the difference, and prevalence is
      not it. Rarity travels with the real cause rather than being it.
    </p>',
    worst$prevalence, fmt(worst$psi_cor_mean),
    fmt(best$psi_cor_mean), best$prevalence,
    n_rarest, format(cell$n_species_fit, big.mark = ","),
    fmt(cell$cor_prev)))
}
```

```{r variance-decomposition}
# The section this replaces asserted a prevalence effect from a banded table.
# With the right predictors it evaporates, and something with far more
# explanatory power takes its place. Everything here is measured, not argued.
oc <- vd$occupancy
oc <- oc[oc$scenario == vd$example_cell & !is.na(oc$share_env), ]

if (nrow(oc) > 0) {
  cr <- function(x) fmt(stats::cor(oc[[x]], oc$psi_cor), 2)
  fit <- stats::lm(psi_cor ~ sd_eta + share_env + share_spat + occ_true,
                   data = oc)
  r2 <- summary(fit)$adj.r.squared

  emit(sprintf('
    <h3>So what does decide whether a species is recovered?</h3>
    <p>
      Each simulated species has its occupancy driven by three things in known
      proportions: the <b>environmental</b> covariates we measured, the
      <b>spatial</b> field, and the <b>latent factors</b> standing in for
      everything we did not measure. The simulator records that split, so it
      can be set against how well each species was then recovered. Over the
      %s species-fits in <code>%s</code>:
    </p>',
    format(nrow(oc), big.mark = ","), vd$example_cell))

  tbl <- data.frame(
    `What varies between species` = c(
      "Share of occupancy driven by measured environment",
      "Share driven by latent factors (the unmeasured part)",
      "How much the species' true occupancy varies across sites",
      "Share driven by the spatial field",
      "How common the species is"),
    `correlation with psi_cor` = c(cr("share_env"), cr("share_lat"),
                                   cr("sd_eta"), cr("share_spat"),
                                   cr("occ_true")),
    check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  cat(html_table(tbl, align_first_left = TRUE))

  q <- prev_cell  # reuse styling; build the latent-share bands
  oc$band <- cut(oc$share_lat, stats::quantile(oc$share_lat, 0:5 / 5),
                 include.lowest = TRUE)
  agg <- aggregate(cbind(psi_cor, share_env, share_lat) ~ band, oc, mean)
  agg$n <- as.integer(table(oc$band))
  names(agg) <- c("latent share (band)", "psi_cor", "share_env", "share_lat", "n")
  cat(html_table(agg[, c("latent share (band)", "n", "share_env",
                         "share_lat", "psi_cor")],
    caption = "Species grouped by how much of their occupancy comes from the unmeasured, latent part of the model.",
    digits = list(`latent share (band)` = 0, n = 0, share_env = 3,
                  share_lat = 3, psi_cor = 3),
    align_first_left = TRUE))

  emit(sprintf('
    <p>
      <strong>A species is recovered well to the extent its distribution is
      driven by covariates you measured.</strong> From %s in the least
      latent-driven fifth to %s in the most: a factor of nearly three, on the
      same model and the same data.
    </p>
    <p>
      The reason is structural rather than a defect. The environmental part of
      the linear predictor is a coefficient shared across every site, so a
      hundred sites all inform it. The latent part is one row per site,
      informed only by that site&rsquo;s own observations, and no amount of
      other sites helps. A species living mostly in the latent part is being
      reconstructed from the weakest-identified piece of the model. The
      ordination is doing its job -- it represents the residual structure -- but
      it cannot localise it site by site.
    </p>
    <p>
      The second effect is a property of the measurement rather than the model:
      a species whose true occupancy barely varies between sites has no pattern
      to find, and the correlation then compares noise with noise. Together
      with the shares above these account for <b>%s</b> of the variation in
      <code>psi_cor</code>; prevalence adds nothing once they are in.
    </p>
    <p>
      <strong>For a real survey this is the actionable finding on this page.</strong>
      occJSDM will place a species well if you measured the covariates that
      actually govern it. A species responding to something you did not measure
      is absorbed into the latent factors and recovered at roughly %s rather
      than %s. That is an argument for covariate choice, not for more sites.
    </p>',
    fmt(agg$psi_cor[1]), fmt(agg$psi_cor[nrow(agg)]),
    pct(r2, 0), fmt(agg$psi_cor[nrow(agg)]), fmt(agg$psi_cor[1])))
}
```

```{=html}

    <h3>The checks these numbers have to pass</h3>
    <p>
      The table above is one snapshot. The test asserts on pooled summaries of it, with
      floors set by running the whole thing under eight different sets of random seeds and
      taking a value comfortably below the worst seen, so a failure means breakage rather
      than an unlucky draw.
    </p>
```

```{r tier2-checks}
# Floors and swept ranges are the constants from test-recovery-occupancy.R,
# which records them as text because they are a record of a measurement (eight
# seed sets, swept once) rather than something recomputed per run. The Result
# column is computed from the same fit shown above, so the table cannot claim a
# pass that the numbers beside it do not support.
chk <- data.frame(
  `What it measures` = c(
    "Estimated occupancy tracking the truth, averaged over species",
    "Species clearing that bar individually",
    "Telling present sites from absent ones",
    "Coverage of the coefficients driving occupancy",
    "Those coefficients tracking their true values"),
  Result = c(fmt(mean(ex$psi_cor)),
             sprintf("%d of %d", sum(ex$psi_cor >= 0.30), nrow(ex)),
             fmt(mean(ex$auc)),
             fmt(mean(ex$drv_cov)),
             fmt(stats::cor(ex$occ_est, ex$occ_true))),
  Floor = c("0.30", as.character(ceiling(nrow(ex) / 2)), "0.60", "0.55", "0.30"),
  Swept = c("0.498-0.753", "7-10", "0.748-0.855", "0.800-1.000", "0.647-0.900"),
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

n_pass <- sum(c(mean(ex$psi_cor) >= 0.30,
                sum(ex$psi_cor >= 0.30) >= ceiling(nrow(ex) / 2),
                mean(ex$auc) >= 0.60,
                mean(ex$drv_cov) >= 0.55,
                stats::cor(ex$occ_est, ex$occ_true) >= 0.30))

cat(html_table(chk,
  caption = sprintf("Asserted quantities. %s on this fit.",
                    if (n_pass == nrow(chk)) "All five pass"
                    else sprintf("%d of %d pass", n_pass, nrow(chk))),
  align_first_left = TRUE))
```

```{=html}
    <p>
      The species are judged pooled rather than each having to pass alone, because a
      per-species floor proved unworkable: across the eight seed sets the worst individual
      species ranged from &minus;0.401 to 0.913, so any threshold strict enough to be worth
      having would fail on ordinary, healthy data. Counting how many clear the bar keeps
      most of what a per-species check would catch without that fragility.
    </p>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>How close are the estimates, across the whole grid?</h2>
    <p>
      One fit cannot separate the model from the dataset. The full study fits 1000 of
      them &mdash; 100 simulated datasets in each of ten scenarios &mdash; and that is
      enough to say how well each kind of parameter is recovered. Source:
      <code>tests/testthat/test-coverage-study.R</code>, run via
      <code>dev/simstudy/run_study.R</code>.
    </p>
```

```{r accuracy-table}
BLOCK_MEANING <- c(
  B = "species responses to environment",
  G = "trait effects",
  p = "detection probability",
  q = "false-positive rate",
  B0 = "species intercepts",
  beta_theta = "collection-covariate effects",
  resid_cor = "species co-occurrence",
  theta0 = "collection baseline",
  sigma_b = "prior scale on species responses")

acc <- vd$accuracy[vd$accuracy$scenario == vd$example_cell, ]
acc <- acc[order(acc$nrmse, na.last = TRUE), ]
acc$what <- BLOCK_MEANING[acc$block]
acc$what[is.na(acc$what)] <- ""

tbl <- data.frame(Parameter = acc$block, `What it is` = acc$what,
                  bias = acc$bias, nRMSE = acc$nrmse, r = acc$r,
                  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

cat(html_table(tbl,
  caption = sprintf(paste("Reference scenario <code>%s</code>, %d datasets.",
                          "<b>nRMSE</b> is the typical error divided by how much",
                          "the true values themselves vary: below 1 the model",
                          "beats guessing the average, above 1 it does not.",
                          "<b>r</b> correlates estimates against truth."),
                    vd$example_cell, vd$R),
  digits = list(Parameter = 0, `What it is` = 0, bias = 3, nRMSE = 3, r = 3),
  flag = function(d, i) !is.na(d$nRMSE[i]) && d$nRMSE[i] >= 0.95,
  lo = function(d, col, i) {
    (col == "nRMSE" && !is.na(d$nRMSE[i]) && d$nRMSE[i] >= 0.95) ||
    (col == "r" && !is.na(d$r[i]) && d$r[i] < 0.40)
  },
  align_first_left = TRUE))
```

```{r accuracy-narrative}
# Classify rather than name. The old prose hard-coded "B and G are recovered
# well" and "resid_cor and theta0 are not", which is a claim about a particular
# run: if a fix lands and a parameter moves between those groups, hand-written
# prose keeps asserting the old grouping while the table above contradicts it.
code <- function(x) paste0("<code>", x, "</code>", collapse = ", ")
lst <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) == 0) return("")
  if (length(x) == 1) return(code(x))
  paste(code(x[-length(x)]), "and", code(x[length(x)]))
}

good <- acc[!is.na(acc$nrmse) & acc$nrmse < 0.70, ]
poor <- acc[!is.na(acc$nrmse) & (acc$nrmse >= 0.95 | acc$r < 0.40), ]
mid  <- acc[!acc$block %in% c(good$block, poor$block), ]

if (nrow(good) > 0) emit(sprintf('
    <p>
      <strong>Best recovered: %s.</strong> %s sit below 0.7 nRMSE, i.e. comfortably
      better than ignoring the data would be, correlating with truth at %s. If you
      are fitting this model to ask which species respond to which environmental
      gradients, that is the part of the answer that holds up.
    </p>',
  lst(good$block),
  if (nrow(good) == 1) "It sits" else "They sit",
  paste(fmt(good$r, 2), collapse = " and ")))

if (nrow(mid) > 0) {
  worst_bias <- mid[which.max(abs(mid$bias)), ]
  emit(sprintf('
    <p>
      <strong>Respectable but not sharp: %s.</strong> These land between 0.7 and
      0.95 nRMSE. The largest bias among them is %s at %s, so that quantity is
      being reported as systematically %s than it is.
    </p>',
    lst(mid$block), code(worst_bias$block), fmt(worst_bias$bias),
    if (worst_bias$bias > 0) "higher" else "lower"))
}

if (nrow(poor) > 0) emit(sprintf('
    <p>
      <strong>Not recovered: %s.</strong> %s nRMSE at or near 1 and correlations
      with truth of %s. For %s, the estimates carry essentially no information
      about the true values -- an nRMSE above 1 is worse than simply predicting
      the overall average. %s covered below.
    </p>',
  lst(poor$block),
  if (nrow(poor) == 1) "It has" else "They have",
  paste(fmt(poor$r, 3), collapse = " and "),
  if (nrow(poor) == 1) "it" else "these",
  if (nrow(poor) == 1) "It is" else "They are"))
```

```{=html}
  <section>
    <h2>What &ldquo;coverage&rdquo; means</h2>
    <p>
      The model doesn&rsquo;t just report a number for, say, species 3&rsquo;s response
      to elevation. It reports a <strong>95% credible interval</strong> &mdash; a range,
      with the claim <em>&ldquo;I&rsquo;m 95% sure the true value is in here.&rdquo;</em>
    </p>
    <p>
      That claim is testable. Simulate 100 datasets where the truth is known, fit all
      100, and for each ask one question: did the interval contain the truth? Then count.
      That count is <strong>coverage</strong>. Falling short of the advertised rate is
      <strong>undercoverage</strong> &mdash; intervals that contain the truth less often
      than they promise, because they are too narrow or sitting off-centre.
    </p>
    <p>
      It matters in print. Report a 95% interval for a parameter that covers at 72%, and
      you are overstating your confidence to a reader who has no way to check.
      Overcoverage &mdash; intervals wider than they need to be &mdash; is the opposite
      problem: safer, but you are discarding power you actually had. And as the section
      above shows, an honest interval around a useless estimate is still useless.
    </p>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>The ten scenarios</h2>
    <p>
      One is the reference design; the other nine each change <strong>exactly one
      thing</strong> about it. When a cell misbehaves, you know which feature caused it.
    </p>
    <p>
      The reference is a mid-sized survey: 100 sites, 10 species, 2 water samples per
      site, 2 primers, 3 PCR replicates each, two environmental covariates, one
      collection covariate, two measured traits, two ordination axes, spatial field on.
      It exercises every feature at once. Definitions:
      <code>tests/testthat/helper-simstudy.R</code>.
    </p>
    <div class="scroller">
      <table>
  <caption>Each variant differs from the reference in one respect only.</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th>Scenario</th><th>What changes</th><th>What it asks</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td class="name">spatial_isolated</td><td>traits off</td><td>Does the spatial term work with trait effects out of the way?</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="name">traits_isolated</td><td>spatial off</td><td>Does the trait&times;environment term work without the spatial field competing?</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="name">primers_3</td><td>2 &rarr; 3 primers</td><td>Does per-primer detection hold with more primers?</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="name">low_information</td><td>40 sites, weak detection</td><td>The hard case: thin, realistic eDNA data.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="name">d_underfit</td><td>truth 4 axes, fit 2</td><td>Under-specifying the ordination &mdash; the common real mistake.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="name">d_overfit</td><td>truth 2 axes, fit 4</td><td>Over-specifying it.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="name">species_20</td><td>10 &rarr; 20 species</td><td>Does it hold as the community grows?</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="name">occupancy</td><td>no PCR stage</td><td>The collapsed form: field replicates only.</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="name">binary</td><td>no replicates</td><td>Pure JSDM, no detection model.</td></tr>
```

```{r tallies}
# Two contrasting parameters from the reference cell: the best-calibrated block
# and the worst. Which two those are is read from the data rather than named,
# so the section keeps making its point if a fix moves them.
ref <- vd$summary[vd$summary$scenario == vd$example_cell, ]
ref <- ref[order(abs(ref$coverage - 0.95)), ]

tally <- function(row, label, note_good, note_bad) {
  hits <- round(100 * row$coverage)
  band <- if (abs(row$coverage - 0.95) <= 0.03) "is-good"
          else if (row$coverage < 0.95) "is-bad" else "is-warn"
  sprintf('
<figure class="tally">
<div class="tally-head">
<div class="tally-label"><b>%s</b> (<code>%s</code>) -- %s</div>
<div class="tally-delta">%d of 100</div>
</div>
<div class="tally-row">
<div class="tally-when">n = %d</div>
<div class="marks" data-hits="%d"></div>
<div class="tally-score %s">%s</div>
</div>
<figcaption class="tally-note">%s</figcaption>
</figure>',
    label, row$block,
    if (band == "is-good") "the interval means what it says"
      else if (band == "is-bad") "overconfident" else "conservative",
    hits, row$n_checked, hits, band, fmt(row$coverage),
    if (band == "is-good") note_good else note_bad)
}

best <- ref[1, ]
worst <- ref[nrow(ref), ]

miss_best <- round(100 * (1 - best$coverage))
miss_worst <- round(100 * (1 - worst$coverage))

emit(sprintf('<div class="tally-set">%s%s</div>',
  tally(best, BLOCK_MEANING[best$block] %||% best$block,
        sprintf(paste("%d misses where five were promised. That is within the",
                      "noise of the measurement, and this is what a calibrated",
                      "parameter looks like."), miss_best),
        sprintf("%d misses against five promised.", miss_best)),
  tally(worst, BLOCK_MEANING[worst$block] %||% worst$block,
        sprintf("%d misses against five promised.", miss_worst),
        sprintf(paste("%d misses against five promised, %s times the advertised",
                      "error rate. A reader quoting these intervals would be",
                      "substantially more confident than the data warrants."),
                miss_worst, fmt(miss_worst / 5, 1)))))
```

````{=html}
      Nominal is 0.95, and at 100 datasets the measurement itself carries a standard error
      of about 0.022, so differences smaller than that are noise.

      <table>
  <caption>Median across scenarios, with the range and the worst-performing cell.</caption>

```{r coverage-summary-table}
cs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(vd$summary, vd$summary$block), function(d) {
  wi <- which.min(d$coverage)
  data.frame(
    Parameter = d$block[1],
    median = stats::median(d$coverage),
    lowest = d$coverage[wi],
    highest = max(d$coverage),
    # Blank rather than naming a cell when every scenario ties, which is what
    # a block pinned at 1.000 everywhere does: there is no worst cell to name.
    `worst cell` = if (diff(range(d$coverage)) < 1e-9) "" else d$scenario[wi],
    check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
cs <- cs[order(cs$median), ]

cat(html_table(cs,
  caption = "Median across scenarios, with the range and the worst-performing cell.",
  digits = list(Parameter = 0, median = 3, lowest = 3, highest = 3,
                `worst cell` = 0),
  flag = function(d, i) d$median[i] < 0.90,
  lo = function(d, col, i) {
    (col == "median" && d$median[i] < 0.90) ||
    (col == "lowest" && d$lowest[i] < 0.85)
  },
  align_first_left = TRUE))
```

```{=html}
</table>
    </div>
    <p>
      <strong>Most of the model is well calibrated.</strong> <code>B</code>,
      <code>G</code>, <code>q</code> and <code>B0</code> all sit within noise of the
      advertised 0.95 in the reference design and in most variants. Combined with the
      accuracy table, <code>B</code> and <code>G</code> are the parts of this model you
      can quote with a straight face.
    </p>
    <p>
      <strong><code>beta_theta</code> is genuinely overconfident.</strong> A median of
      0.757 against a promised 0.95 means roughly one interval in four misses when one in
      twenty should. This is a real defect, localised to the collection-covariate slopes,
      and it is open.
    </p>
    <p>
      <strong><code>theta0</code> overcovers at 0.982.</strong> Safe rather than
      dangerous, but read it alongside the accuracy table: those wide intervals sit around
      estimates that correlate with truth at 0.342. Honest about being uninformative.
    </p>
    <p>
      <strong><code>sigma_b</code> reads 1.000 everywhere</strong> because its prior is
      tight enough to dominate the data. It is not evidence of anything.
    </p>

    <div class="finding">
      <h3>Do not read the <code>resid_cor</code> row as undercoverage</h3>
      <p>
        It looks like the second-worst calibrated parameter in the table. It is something
        stranger, and the number should not be quoted as evidence for or against anything
        until the measurement is repaired.
      </p>
````

```{r resid-cor-degeneracy}
dg <- vd$degeneracy
ref_dg <- dg[dg$scenario == vd$example_cell, ]
alt_dg <- dg[dg$scenario != vd$example_cell, ]
alt_dg <- alt_dg[which.max(alt_dg$predicted_coverage), ]
rc <- vd$accuracy[vd$accuracy$scenario == vd$example_cell &
                  vd$accuracy$block == "resid_cor", ]

emit(sprintf('
      <p>
        The credible intervals for residual correlations span almost the entire range
        a correlation can occupy: <strong>%s are wider than 1.9</strong> on a scale
        bounded by -1 and 1, median width %s. An interval that wide contains
        everything, so coverage should be near perfect. It is %s only because %s of
        the true correlations sit at exactly &plusmn;1, right on the boundary, and
        fall a hair outside.
      </p>
      <p>
        Coverage here is therefore <em>arithmetically</em> one minus the share of true
        correlations equal to &plusmn;1: %s predicted against %s measured in the
        reference cell, and %s against %s in <code>%s</code>. That difference is a
        property of the simulation, not of the model -- with two ordination axes each
        species is a two-dimensional vector and many pairs come out exactly collinear;
        with four that is rare.
      </p>
      <p>
        The honest summary is the accuracy table: residual correlations correlate with
        truth at <strong>%s</strong>. They are not being recovered, and the intervals
        are too wide rather than too narrow. If species co-occurrence is what you came
        for, this configuration of the model does not deliver it, and
        <code>plotResidualCorrelationMatrix()</code> should be read with that in mind.
      </p>',
  pct(ref_dg$share_wide, 1), fmt(ref_dg$median_width),
  fmt(ref_dg$coverage), pct(ref_dg$share_at_one, 0),
  fmt(ref_dg$predicted_coverage), fmt(ref_dg$coverage),
  fmt(alt_dg$predicted_coverage), fmt(alt_dg$coverage), alt_dg$scenario,
  fmt(rc$r)))
```

```{r breakdown}
# Find the worst cell from the data rather than asserting it is
# low_information. If a fix changes which configuration fails hardest, the
# prose should follow the numbers instead of contradicting them.
worst_row <- vd$summary[which.min(vd$summary$coverage), ]
wc <- vd$summary[vd$summary$scenario == worst_row$scenario, ]
wc <- wc[order(wc$coverage), ]
wacc <- vd$accuracy[vd$accuracy$scenario == worst_row$scenario, ]
bias_of <- function(b) {
  v <- wacc$bias[wacc$block == b]
  if (length(v) == 0) NA_real_ else v[1]
}
others <- utils::head(wc$block[-1], 2)

emit(sprintf('
    <p>
      <strong>The hardest cell is <code>%s</code>.</strong> There <code>%s</code>
      covers at <strong>%s</strong> against a nominal 0.95, with a bias of %s.
      Everything downstream of it degrades in the same cell: %s. This is the
      configuration to look at before trusting the model on a small survey.
    </p>',
  worst_row$scenario, worst_row$block, fmt(worst_row$coverage),
  fmt(bias_of(worst_row$block)),
  paste(sprintf("<code>%s</code> covers at %s", others,
                fmt(wc$coverage[match(others, wc$block)])),
        collapse = " and ")))

emit(sprintf('
    <p>
      <strong>These are one run at one seed.</strong> Every number here comes from a
      single execution of the study, %d replicates per cell, so the coverage figures
      carry a standard error near %s. The occupancy statistics are the exception:
      those now come with the spread across all %s species-fits shown above, rather
      than resting on the single fit at the top.
    </p>',
  vd$R, fmt(sqrt(0.95 * 0.05 / vd$R), 3),
  format(sum(vd$occupancy_summary$n_species_fit), big.mark = ",")))
```

```{r sites-comparison, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 9.5, dev = "png", dpi = 160}
ex <- vd$extra_cells[["sites_300"]]
if (!is.null(ex)) {
  b <- vd$occupancy[vd$occupancy$scenario == vd$example_cell &
                    !is.na(vd$occupancy$share_lat), ]
  s <- ex$occupancy[!is.na(ex$occupancy$share_lat), ]
  q <- function(x, p) as.numeric(stats::quantile(x, p))

  emit(sprintf('
    <h3>Does a bigger survey help?</h3>
    <p>
      The same design with <b>three times the sites</b>, 300 against 100, and
      everything else held: same species, same samples per site, same primers,
      same PCR replicates. %s replicates each, so this is a comparison between
      two distributions rather than between two fits.
    </p>
    <p>
      The means move from <b>%s</b> to <b>%s</b>. That understates it, because
      the gain is not spread evenly: the top of the range hardly shifts (%s to
      %s at the 95th percentile, since those species were already near the
      ceiling) while the bottom moves a long way (%s to %s at the 5th). The
      share of species-fits coming out below 0.3 -- effectively unusable --
      falls from <b>%s</b> to <b>%s</b>.
    </p>
    <p>
      So what a bigger survey buys is not that every species is placed better.
      It is that <strong>far fewer species come out unusable</strong>, which for
      a real survey is the more valuable guarantee. Note also that both
      distributions are strongly left-skewed with a tail below zero, so a mean
      on its own always flatters this quantity.
    </p>',
    format(ex$R %||% 100, big.mark = ","),
    fmt(mean(b$psi_cor), 2), fmt(mean(s$psi_cor), 2),
    fmt(q(b$psi_cor, .95), 2), fmt(q(s$psi_cor, .95), 2),
    fmt(q(b$psi_cor, .05), 2), fmt(q(s$psi_cor, .05), 2),
    pct(mean(b$psi_cor < 0.3), 0), pct(mean(s$psi_cor < 0.3), 0)))

  print(plot_sites_distribution())

  emit(sprintf('
    <p>
      The panels below the first split species by how much of their occupancy
      the model can see directly. The shift is modest where occupancy is
      governed by measured covariates and largest where it is governed by the
      unmeasured, latent part -- the band where the 100-site distribution has
      real mass at and below zero. More sites sharpen the shared loadings that
      the latent pathway depends on, which is why the species with the least
      directly usable information gain the most.
    </p>
    <p>
      One thing this does <em>not</em> buy: calibration. In the same comparison
      <code>beta_theta</code> coverage falls from %s to %s. More data makes the
      estimates better and that parameter&rsquo;s intervals more confidently
      wrong, which is the open issue described further down.
    </p>',
    fmt(vd$summary$coverage[vd$summary$scenario == vd$example_cell &
                            vd$summary$block == "beta_theta"]),
    fmt(ex$summary$coverage[ex$summary$block == "beta_theta"])))
}
```

```{=html}
    <h2>What runs when</h2>
    <div class="tiers">
      <div class="tier">
        <div class="tier-when">10&nbsp;sec<br>every&nbsp;run</div>
        <div class="tier-body">
          <h3>Does it work at all?</h3>
          <p>
            Fits every configuration the package offers &mdash; two-stage,
            occupancy-only, pure JSDM, with and without traits or spatial structure &mdash;
            and checks each completes and returns sensibly shaped output. One test per bug
            already fixed, named after it, so none returns unnoticed. Plus the convergence
            diagnostics, checked against values worked out by hand.
            <code>test-smoke-configs.R</code>, <code>test-api-contracts.R</code>,
            <code>test-regression-bugs.R</code>, <code>test-diagnostics.R</code>.
          </p>
          <p>
            Checks <em>shape</em> rather than exact numbers, because any legitimate change
            to the sampler moves every number and a suite of stored values would turn each
            such change into a wall of meaningless failures. It is also partly forced: the
            model reproduces exactly from a seed on one processor core but not on several,
            since work goes to whichever core is free first and that order varies. Results
            are unaffected, but a run that must be repeated exactly has to be pinned, and
            two tests are.
          </p>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="tier">
        <div class="tier-when">30&nbsp;sec<br>local&nbsp;only</div>
        <div class="tier-body">
          <h3>Has anything obviously broken?</h3>
          <p>
            Five simulated datasets fitted and compared against known truth, plus the
            per-species occupancy check at the top of this page. Too few to measure
            coverage &mdash; these are canaries. Their job is catching a broken connection
            between truth and estimate, which shows up as coverage near zero rather than
            merely low. <code>test-recovery.R</code>,
            <code>test-recovery-occupancy.R</code>.
          </p>
        </div>
      </div>
```

```{r tier3-runtime}
          </p>
          <p>
            Each fit is single-threaded; the parallelism is across replicate
```

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  // Lay out each tally as 100 marks. Misses are spread by a fixed stride
  // rather than randomised, so the figures stay visually comparable and the
  // page renders identically every time. Scoped to this article's marks only.
  document.querySelectorAll('.occjsdm-report .marks').forEach(function (el) {
    var hits = parseInt(el.dataset.hits, 10);
    var misses = 100 - hits;
    var stride = misses > 0 ? 100 / misses : Infinity;
    var next = stride / 2;
    var frag = document.createDocumentFragment();

    for (var i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
      var d = document.createElement('div');
      var isMiss = misses > 0 && i >= Math.floor(next);
      if (isMiss) { next += stride; }
      d.className = 'mark ' + (isMiss ? 'miss' : 'hit');
      frag.appendChild(d);
    }
    el.appendChild(frag);
  });
})();
</script>
```
